title: Broomstick lace — forming the loops
subtitle: Draw each stitch up onto a large dowel or thick knitting needle to set the loop size
excerpt: Broomstick lace works in two passes. The first pass draws each crochet loop up and places it on a large-diameter dowel — traditionally a broomstick handle. This sets all the loops to the same large, even size. The second pass groups and works the loops together. This tutorial covers the loop-forming pass.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — broomstick crochet (called 'peacock stitch' and 'pin crochet' in early sources). Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 3 (1888) — broomstick loop formation.

glossaryTerms.definition: A large-diameter dowel, thick knitting needle (15-25 mm), or purpose-made broomstick lace pin used to hold the oversized loops during the loop-forming pass of broomstick lace. The diameter of the pin sets the size of the finished loop groups.

An oversized crochet loop stretched out and placed on the broomstick pin to set its size. A row of broomstick loops is formed in one pass; the next pass works groups of loops together. The loops always come in groups (usually 4 or 5).

content.text: Broomstick lace produces open fan-shaped clusters from loops stretched to a uniform large size. The first pass draws each loop out onto a
— a thick dowel or large knitting needle — to set the size. The second pass (covered in the Broomstick cluster tutorial) groups and works those
into fans. This tutorial covers the loop pass only.

attrs.title: Choosing the pin size
attrs.body: The pin diameter controls the finished fan size. A 15 mm needle makes smaller, tighter fans; a 25 mm dowel makes large, open ones. For DK weight, a 20 mm needle or knitting needle size 20 is a standard starting point. The loops must be large enough to slip on and off the pin easily without stretching the yarn.

content.text: Work a foundation row of dc. Hold the broomstick pin in the left hand (or tuck it under the left arm).
At the end of the dc row, keep the last loop on the crochet hook. Slip this loop onto the broomstick pin — do not remove the hook.
Insert the crochet hook into the next dc of the row, yarn over, draw up a loop and extend it to the size of the pin. Slip this loop onto the pin alongside the first.
Continue: insert, draw up a loop, extend to pin size, slip onto pin. Repeat across the entire row. All loops now sit on the pin in a row.

items.symptom: Loops are uneven — some large, some small
items.cause: Drawing up each loop to a different length rather than consistently to the pin diameter
items.fix: Use the pin as a physical size gauge. Each loop must reach across the full diameter of the pin before sliding it on — do not let the loop seat on the pin until it's big enough.

content.text: The Broomstick cluster tutorial covers working off the loops in groups — the second pass that completes the broomstick lace fabric. Once the two passes are combined, the full fan pattern emerges.
